2230:
A bruise is a dark, discolored patch that appears on the surface of something — most often human skin — after it has been hit or struck hard, without the surface being cut open or broken.

Think of it this way: when something hits you hard enough to hurt, but not hard enough to break your skin, a bruise is what gets left behind.

To truly understand a bruise, you need to understand what happens beneath the surface.

Your skin is like a covering over a vast network of tiny blood vessels called capillaries. These are extremely thin, fragile tubes that carry blood throughout your body.

When you are hit by something — say, you bang your knee against a table — the force of the impact travels through your skin and damages these small blood vessels underneath. They crack or burst. Blood leaks out of them and into the surrounding tissue (the soft material under your skin).

Here is the key point: your skin has not been cut, so this leaked blood has nowhere to escape. It stays trapped under your skin, pooling in one place. It is this pool of blood sitting under your skin that you see as a bruise.
What a Bruise Looks, Feels, and Acts Like

Color: A bruise is not always the same color. It goes through a series of color changes as it heals, because the blood trapped under your skin gradually breaks down:

  • Right after the injury: It may look red or pinkish, since the blood is fresh.
  • Within a day or two: It darkens into blue, purple, or almost black. This is the stage most people recognize as a bruise.
  • As it heals: It fades to green, then yellow, then disappears entirely as your body reabsorbs the blood.

Feel: A bruise is almost always tender — meaning it hurts or aches when you press on it, even gently. The area may also feel slightly swollen or raised.

Size and shape: Bruises can range from a tiny dot to a large patch covering several inches of skin. The harder or more forceful the blow, the larger and darker the bruise tends to be.

Healing: Bruises heal on their own. No blood escapes the body — your body simply breaks down and reabsorbs the leaked blood over time. A typical bruise disappears within two to four weeks.

The word "bruise" (as a noun) is used in a few distinct but related ways:

1. A skin bruise — the most common meaning. Exactly as described above: a discolored, tender patch on your skin from a bump or blow. Also called a contusion in medical language.

2. A bone bruise — when the force of an impact damages the tissue inside a bone without actually cracking or breaking the bone. You cannot see it from the outside, but it causes deep, persistent pain. It is more serious than a skin bruise.

3. An internal bruise (internal bleeding / hematoma) — sometimes a bruise forms deep inside the body, around organs, where it cannot be seen at all. This is medically more serious, since a large amount of blood can pool internally. A hematoma is a specific medical word for a significant collection of blood under the skin or inside the body.

4. A bruise on fruit or vegetables — when an apple, banana, or other soft fruit is knocked, dropped, or squeezed too hard, it develops a soft, brown, mushy, discolored spot. This is also called a bruise. The tissue of the fruit has been damaged, just as body tissue is damaged in a human bruise.

5. A figurative bruise — in everyday language, people sometimes use "bruise" to describe emotional hurt. For example: "That harsh criticism left a bruise on his confidence." Here, it means a wound to someone's feelings, pride, or self-esteem — something that hurt and left a lasting mark, even if not a physical one.

• Contusion — the formal medical term for a bruise on the body. Means exactly the same thing.
  • Hematoma — a more severe form where blood collects in a distinct pocket or lump under the skin or inside the body.
  • Black and blue — a common phrase used to describe the appearance of a heavily bruised area.
  • Tender — how a bruise feels when touched; sore but not from a cut.

A bruise is the visible, painful mark left on skin (or deep inside the body) when a blow damages blood vessels beneath the surface without cutting it open. The dark color comes from blood that leaked out of those vessels and got trapped under the skin. It hurts when pressed, changes color as it heals, and eventually disappears on its own. The word can also describe similar damage to fruit, or emotional damage to a person's pride or feelings.
2231: When something hits, presses, or impacts a surface with enough force to cause hidden damage — damage that you can feel or see, but that doesn't break the outer layer open — that action is called bruising. Think of it as injuring something from the inside, while the surface stays closed.
Sense 1 — To injure a body part by blunt impact

This is the most common and important meaning. When you knock part of your body against something hard — say, you bump your shin against a table — the tiny blood vessels just beneath your skin get crushed and start to leak blood into the surrounding tissue. The skin itself doesn't break or bleed outward, but a dark patch (usually red, purple, blue, or yellowish) appears under it. The action that caused this is described using the verb bruise.

"She bruised her knee when she tripped on the stairs."

"He bruised his arm after the fall."

Notice that the verb here is transitive — one thing is doing the bruising, and a body part is receiving it. But bruise can also be used intransitively, meaning you can say that a person or body part bruises without specifying what caused it:

"She bruises easily." (meaning her skin develops bruise marks with very little force)

"Fair-skinned people tend to bruise more visibly."

You can also bruise things that aren't soft tissue — bones, for example. A bruised rib means the bone was hit hard enough to damage it internally, but it wasn't cracked or broken.
Sense 2 — To damage the surface of soft objects, especially fruit

This sense works exactly like the physical body sense, just applied to objects. When a soft fruit like a peach, banana, or apple gets knocked, dropped, or pressed against something hard, the outer skin stays intact but the flesh just beneath it gets crushed and discoloured — it turns soft, dark, and mushy in that spot. That is bruising.

"The mangoes got bruised in the bag during transport."

"Handle the peaches carefully so you don't bruise them."

"These tomatoes are bruised — they won't last long."
Sense 3 — To hurt someone emotionally or damage their confidence

The verb bruise is also used figuratively to describe emotional or psychological harm. Just like a physical bruise is damage beneath the surface that isn't always immediately visible, emotional bruising refers to a kind of hurt that goes deep but isn't always obvious to others. It often involves a person's feelings, pride, ego, or self-esteem.

"His cold rejection bruised her feelings."

"Losing the competition bruised his ego."

"Years of criticism had bruised her confidence."

Notice something important here: this sense implies a moderate kind of emotional hurt — deeper than a slight sting, but not completely devastating. It suggests damage, not total destruction. You wouldn't typically say someone's spirit was "bruised" if they were utterly broken — you'd use stronger words for that.
Sense 4 — To crush or press lightly (especially in cooking)

This is a more specialised but legitimate use of the verb. In cooking, when you bruise an ingredient like lemongrass, garlic, ginger, or a herb, you press or lightly crush it — usually with the flat side of a knife, a pestle, or the back of a spoon — just enough to break its fibers slightly and release its oils, juices, or aroma. You're not grinding it to a paste; you're doing something gentler. The ingredient remains mostly intact but is just damaged enough to release its flavour.

"Bruise the garlic cloves before adding them to the pan."

"Bruise the lemongrass stalks to release their fragrance."
The One Thread Running Through All Senses

Every use of bruise as a verb carries the same underlying logic: the outer layer stays whole, but damage happens beneath it or within it. Whether it's your skin, a fruit's peel, a person's dignity, or an herb's fibers — bruising is always about impact or pressure causing internal or hidden damage without an outright break or rupture. That is what makes it distinct from words like cut, tear, or shatter, all of which involve something being broken open or apart.

These are common word combinations you'll frequently encounter with this verb:

"Badly bruised" — seriously injured or hurt (physically or emotionally).
"Bruised and battered" — a common phrase describing something or someone that has taken a lot of damage over time.
"Bruised ego/pride" — the figurative use, referring to wounded self-esteem.
"Bruise easily" — to be prone to bruising, either physically or emotionally.

To bruise means to cause injury, damage, or harm to something (a body part, an object, a feeling, or an ingredient) through pressure, impact, or force, in a way where the surface stays unbroken but the inside is damaged. It works literally on bodies and soft objects, figuratively on emotions and pride, and specifically in cooking to mean a gentle crush that releases flavour.
2232:
To bruit something means to spread a piece of news, a rumor, or a report widely among people — usually in an informal, word-of-mouth way, and often before anything has been officially confirmed.

Think of it as the act of something being whispered around, passed from person to person, or circulating through the air in a community. The information travels fast, touches many ears, but doesn't come from any single, official announcement.

This word almost never appears alone. It comes paired with the word "about" (and sometimes the older word "abroad," which here means "widely" or "out into the world" — not "in a foreign country").

The most natural constructions are:

  • "It is bruited about that..."
  • "It was bruited about that..."
  • "...bruited abroad..."

You'll also notice it almost always appears in the passive voice — meaning you rarely say "She bruited the news." Instead, the news itself is the subject: "The news was bruited about." This reflects how the word actually works: nobody is clearly in charge of spreading it. It just... spreads, the way a rumor does.

"It was bruited about the town that the old manor house had finally been sold."

Here, nobody made an official announcement. People were just talking, whispering, passing it along — and the news spread everywhere.

"Word was bruited abroad that the general intended to resign."

Again — no press conference, no statement. Just information moving quietly but widely through a community, a court, a city.

"Long before any official statement, it had been bruited about the office that layoffs were coming."

This shows the common situation where something is bruited: before the official word arrives. The rumor travels first.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

This is an important layer. "Bruit" carries several subtle feelings with it:

  • Unofficial-ness. What is bruited hasn't been confirmed. It exists in the zone between rumor and fact.
  • Wideness. It isn't told to just one person in secret. It spreads broadly — throughout a town, a court, a company, a social circle.
  • Informality. Nobody is announcing it from a podium. It travels through conversation, gossip, and hearsay.
  • A slight air of mystery or intrigue. Because the source is unclear and the information unverified, there's often a sense that something significant is afoot, even if unconfirmed.

Crucially, something bruited about isn't necessarily false — it may turn out to be completely true. The word describes how information spreads, not whether it's accurate.
Register: When Do People Use This Word?

"Bruit" is a formal and literary word. You won't hear it in casual everyday conversation. You'll encounter it in:

  • Literature and historical writing
  • Journalism (especially more literary or elevated journalism)
  • Legal or formal contexts
  • Academic writing

In everyday speech, the same idea would be expressed as: "Word got around that...", "Rumor has it that...", or "People were saying that..."

Choosing to use "bruit" instead of these everyday phrases signals a more elevated, precise, or old-fashioned style.
How It's Different from Similar Words

IdeaEveryday Word"Bruit" adds...
Spreading news"spread," "circulate"the sense of informality + lack of clear source
Rumors"rumor has it," "gossip"more formality and gravitas
Whispering around"word got out"a broader, wider reach

Actually — you asked for no tables, so to put it plainly: "spread" and "circulate" are neutral and general. "Gossip" implies the content is trivial or malicious. "Bruit" sits in the middle — it's serious in tone, suggests wide informal circulation, and carries the implication that the source is unclear or unofficial.
To bruit something about is to cause a piece of news or a rumor to spread widely and informally among people — often before any official confirmation, and with no single clearly identified source.

Imagine a crowd all murmuring the same thing to each other. Nobody knows exactly who started it or if it's true, but somehow everyone has heard it. That buzzing, spreading, unofficial circulation of information — that is what "bruit" captures in a single word.
2233: Brumal means of, relating to, or characteristic of winter. It's a single-word way to say "wintry" — but with a richer, more deliberate feel.

When you call something brumal, you are saying it belongs to winter, or that it carries the deep qualities of winter. Not just cold, but the full atmosphere of the season: short, dark days; long, silent nights; frost on the ground; bare trees; grey skies; and the kind of stillness and austerity that only the coldest months bring.

Think of it as a label that stamps something with the essence of winter.

Almost anything that can carry the character or feel of winter:

Weather and atmosphere — A brumal wind is not just a cold wind; it is a wind that feels distinctly wintry, the kind that bites and howls in January. Brumal gloom refers to the heavy, sunless, oppressive quality of winter skies.

Landscapes and scenes — A brumal landscape is one that looks like winter owns it: bare fields, frozen ponds, leafless branches, perhaps snow. The word paints the entire picture at once.

Time periods — You can refer to the brumal months (typically December, January, February in the Northern Hemisphere) to mean the winter months.

Feelings and moods — Writers sometimes use brumal to describe a mood or emotional atmosphere that mirrors winter — cold, bleak, withdrawn, austere. A brumal silence, for example, suggests a deep, heavy, winter-like quiet.
The Tone and Weight of the Word

This is important: brumal is not the word you use in casual conversation. You would not say to a friend, "Wow, it's pretty brumal outside!" That would sound strange and out of place.

Brumal is a formal, literary word — the kind you find in poetry, literary novels, and thoughtful essays. It carries an air of elegance and precision. When a writer chooses "brumal" over "wintry," they are making a deliberate, refined choice. They want the word to feel weighty, atmospheric, and a little timeless.
How "Brumal" Differs from Just Saying "Cold" or "Wintry"

These distinctions matter:

Cold is about temperature alone. A refrigerator is cold. Brumal is never just about temperature.

Wintry is the plain, everyday equivalent of brumal. They mean essentially the same thing, but brumal is more elevated, more poetic, and more intentional in tone.

Brumal is specific to winter as a whole season — its atmosphere, its character, its mood. It does not simply mean low temperature; it means winter-ness in the fullest sense.

These will show you the word in action:

  • "A brumal quiet had settled over the town, as though even the birds had given up on sound."
  • "She gazed out at the brumal landscape — grey, bare, and utterly still."
  • "The brumal months always brought him a kind of melancholy he could not shake."
  • "There was something brumal about his expression — cold, distant, stripped of warmth."
  • "The poem captures the brumal beauty of a January dawn, when frost coats every surface and the world holds its breath."

Notice how in the last example, brumal is used alongside "beauty" — this is key. The word does not always mean something negative. Winter has its own austere, clean, quiet beauty, and brumal can capture that too.

Most of the time, brumal carries a slightly melancholic or solemn undertone. Winter, in literature and in life, is often associated with withdrawal, hardship, introspection, and waiting. When writers use brumal, they often intend to evoke those feelings alongside the literal wintry imagery. So the word does double duty: it describes the physical reality of winter and hints at the emotional weight that comes with it.
One Word to Compare It To

Its closest relative is hibernal, which also means "of or relating to winter." They are nearly interchangeable, but hibernal tends to appear more in scientific or technical contexts (like describing animals that hibernate), while brumal leans more toward literary and descriptive use.
Brumal = having the qualities, character, or atmosphere of winter — used as a formal, literary adjective to describe anything that feels deeply, essentially wintry.
2234:
Brume means mist or fog — specifically the kind that is thick, heavy, and low-hanging, the sort that wraps around a landscape like a grey blanket and makes it difficult to see clearly.

Think of a cold, damp morning by the sea, where a pale grey haze sits heavily over the water and the distant shoreline seems to disappear into nothing. That atmospheric, obscuring, moody vapour is a brume.
How It Feels (The Atmosphere of the Word)

This is where "brume" becomes interesting. It isn't just any fog. The word carries a specific feeling with it:

  • Heavy and dense, not light and wispy
  • Cold and damp, not warm and summery
  • Gloomy and mysterious, not gentle and romantic
  • Still and oppressive, as if the world has been muffled

When writers use "brume," they want you to feel the weight of the air, the silence it creates, and the way it obscures and hides things. It has a slightly eerie, melancholic quality to it.
How It Differs from Similar Words

English has several words for atmospheric water vapour in the air — mist, fog, haze, and brume — and they are close but not identical.

  • Mist is light, thin, and gentle. It softens a landscape. You can still see through it fairly well. A morning mist often burns away as the sun rises.
  • Fog is thicker than mist. It reduces visibility significantly and feels heavier. It's common and practical.
  • Haze is often caused by heat, dust, or smoke — not necessarily water vapour. It makes things look blurry and distant.
  • Brume overlaps most with fog and thick mist, but it goes further in feel. It implies something denser, darker, colder, and more atmospheric than plain "fog." It's the fog of a gloomy winter shoreline, a brooding sea, a silenced forest at dawn.

In short, all brumes are fog or mist, but not all fog or mist is a brume.
What Kind of Word It Is (Register)

"Brume" is a literary and poetic word. You will almost never hear it in everyday conversation. Nobody walks into a coffee shop and says, "Awful brume out there today." They say fog or mist.

You will encounter "brume" in:

  • Poetry — where writers want a single evocative word to suggest cold, mystery, and atmosphere
  • Literary prose — novels and essays that aim for a rich, elevated style
  • Descriptive writing — travel writing, nature writing, or any writing meant to paint a vivid atmospheric picture

Knowing this is important. Using "brume" in casual speech would sound odd, even pretentious. But reading it in a literary context, you now know it signals something thick, cold, heavy, and moody in the air.

Here are a few sentences showing how the word is used naturally:

  • The harbour had vanished entirely behind a grey brume that rolled in from the ocean before sunrise.
  • She could barely make out the old lighthouse through the brume that clung to the cliffs.
  • A winter brume settled over the valley, and the village below disappeared as if it had never existed.
  • He stood at the window, watching the brume drift silently through the empty streets.

Notice in each case: there is coldness, poor visibility, a heavy atmosphere, and a sense of mood — not just neutral description.

If you ever see the word brumous, it is the adjective form, meaning full of brume — foggy, misty, wintry, and gloomy. A brumous morning is a cold, fog-heavy, overcast one. It is just as literary and rare as "brume" itself.
A One-Sentence Summary to Remember It Forever

Brume is a literary word for a thick, heavy, cold mist or fog — the kind that feels gloomy and atmospheric, wraps around landscapes, and obscures everything, especially near water or in winter.

Whenever you see it, picture a cold grey sea with dense fog hanging silently over the water, hiding what lies beyond. That image will never lead you wrong.
2235:
Brunt means the main force, worst impact, or heaviest burden of something difficult or harmful.

Think of it this way: when something bad happens — a storm, an attack, someone's anger, a financial crisis — that bad thing doesn't always hit everyone equally. Usually, someone or something gets hit the hardest. That hardest, heaviest, most intense part of the blow is the brunt.
The Most Important Thing to Know About This Word

"Brunt" is almost never used alone. You will almost always see it in one fixed pattern:

bear / take / feel / suffer the brunt of (something)

This phrase means: to receive the worst, most intense, or most damaging part of something.
Examples That Show the Meaning Clearly

1. A natural disaster:

"The small fishing village bore the brunt of the hurricane."

The hurricane hit many places, but that village got hit the hardest. Other areas got some wind and rain — that village got the full, terrible force of it.

2. Anger:

"When the boss came in furious, the new employee bore the brunt of his anger."

The boss was angry at everyone, but the new employee received the worst of it — the sharpest, most intense part of that anger.

3. A financial crisis:

"During the recession, the poor bore the brunt of the economic collapse."

Many people were affected, but the poor suffered the most severely — the heaviest, cruelest part of it fell on them.

4. War:

"The front-line soldiers took the brunt of the enemy's attack."

The attack struck many positions, but the soldiers at the front felt the full, concentrated force of it.
The Three Key Ideas Hidden Inside "Brunt"

Understanding these three ideas will make the word permanently clear in your mind:

1. It is the WORST or MOST INTENSE part.
Not just any part of something difficult — the heaviest part. If a storm causes problems across a whole country, the "brunt" is where the destruction was most severe, not where it merely rained a little harder.

2. It is UNEQUAL.
The word always carries the idea that the impact is not spread evenly. Someone or something is carrying a disproportionate share of the difficulty. This is why we say someone "bears" the brunt — because they are carrying a load that is heavier than what others carry.

3. It is almost always something NEGATIVE.
You will never hear "she bore the brunt of the celebration" or "he took the brunt of the good news." Brunt is reserved for hardship — attacks, criticism, disasters, anger, suffering, blame.

Imagine five people standing in a row during a powerful rainstorm with strong wind. The person at the front of the row gets completely soaked and almost knocked over — rain in the face, full wind force, everything. The people behind are sheltered and barely feel the wind at all.

That person at the front is bearing the brunt of the storm. They are receiving its main, concentrated, most powerful force.
Shades of Meaning — When to Use It

You can use "brunt" for physical things:

  • The brunt of a punch, a blast, a storm, a crash.

You can use it for non-physical things:

  • The brunt of someone's anger, criticism, blame, or frustration.
  • The brunt of a financial burden, a health crisis, or a social problem.

The word works in both cases because the idea is the same: the hardest part is landing on you.

• It does not mean all of something. It means the worst or main part.
    "She bore the brunt of his anger" doesn't mean nobody else felt it — it means she felt it the most.
  • It does not simply mean result or consequence. It specifically means the most forceful, most concentrated, most intense part of an impact.
  • It is not the same as burden alone. A burden is simply a heavy load. Brunt is specifically about being on the receiving end of the sharpest force of something.
The Complete Picture in One Sentence

Brunt is the main and most intense force of something harmful or difficult, and when you "bear the brunt" of something, you are the one who absorbs the worst of it — more than anyone else.

Once you remember that person standing at the front of the row in the storm, you will never forget this word.
2236: The word brush has several distinct meanings. Think of them as separate "identities" the same word carries. Here they are, one by one.

This is the most common meaning. A brush is a tool that has:

  • a handle (the part you hold), and
  • bristles attached to one end — stiff fibers made from hair, nylon, plant fibers, wire, or similar materials.

The bristles do the actual work: they spread, scrub, sweep, or smooth.

Brushes are made in many sizes and shapes for different jobs:

  • A paintbrush has soft bristles to carry and spread paint onto a surface.
  • A toothbrush has short, firm bristles to scrub your teeth.
  • A hairbrush has bristles (often with rounded tips) to smooth and untangle hair.
  • A scrubbing brush has stiff, tough bristles for heavy cleaning — like scrubbing a floor.
  • A makeup brush has very soft, fine bristles for applying powder or blush to skin.
  • A pastry brush (used in cooking) has soft bristles to spread butter, oil, or egg wash onto food.

So whenever you see the word "brush" used as a tool, ask: What is it spreading, cleaning, or grooming? That will tell you which kind it is.

A brush can also mean a gentle, fleeting contact — when something just barely grazes or skims across a surface.

She felt the brush of cold wind against her cheek.
He walked past her, and she felt the brush of his sleeve against her arm.

Notice that in this sense, the contact is:

  • light (not heavy or firm),
  • quick (over in a moment), and
  • almost accidental or delicate.

This meaning comes naturally from watching how a brush moves — it sweeps lightly, not heavily.

When something dangerous, serious, or unwanted comes very close to happening — but just barely — we call it a brush with that thing.

He had a brush with death when the car nearly hit him.
She had a brush with the law after the argument got out of hand.
The company had a brush with bankruptcy last year.

Think of it like this: danger or trouble came close enough to graze you — like a brush stroke across your life — but didn't fully hit. The word captures that sense of a narrow escape or a close, uncomfortable moment.

This meaning is very common in everyday English. You will hear "a brush with _" used to describe near-misses, brief encounters with authority, or moments where something serious almost happened.

In outdoor and nature contexts, brush refers to an area of dense, tangled, low-growing plants — bushes, shrubs, small trees, and wild undergrowth. It's the kind of thick, messy vegetation you might find in forests, countryside, or wilderness areas.

The deer disappeared into the brush.
They cleared the brush from the hillside to prevent wildfires.
The children found a bird's nest hidden in the brush.

This sense is especially common in American English. You might also hear brushwood, which means the cut branches, twigs, and small woody stems cleared from such an area.

The key idea here: it's not a forest of tall trees, and not a neat garden. It's wild, low, tangled, and dense.

In the world of fox hunting, the bushy tail of a fox has a specific name: it is called a brush. This is a specialized term used by hunters and in literature about hunting.

The fox's brush swept through the grass as it ran.

This meaning is narrow — you will mainly encounter it in hunting contexts or classic British literature. But it's worth knowing so you're not confused when you see it.

In engineering and technology, a brush (sometimes called a carbon brush) is a small block or pad — usually made of carbon or graphite — that presses against a rotating part inside an electric motor or generator. Its job is to transfer electrical current between the stationary part and the moving part of the machine.

The motor stopped working because the brushes had worn down.

You'll encounter this meaning if you read about electric motors, generators, or machinery. The name comes from the earliest versions of these components, which literally looked like brushes.

MeaningThe core idea
A tool with bristlesSpreads, cleans, or smooths
A light touchA barely-there, fleeting contact
A brief encounterComing close to something dangerous or serious
Wild undergrowthThick, tangled, low shrubs in nature
A fox's tailSpecialized hunting term
An electrical componentConducts current in a rotating machine

If you look carefully, most meanings of brush share one idea at their heart: a brief, light, sweeping contact. A brush (tool) makes short sweeping strokes. A brush (touch) is a quick, light graze. A brush (encounter) is a fleeting, glancing contact with something serious. Even the image of wild brush — scraggly, loose, sprawling — has that same loose, un-heavy quality.

Once you feel that central idea — something light, brief, and sweeping — the word will feel natural and connected across all its uses.
2237:
Step 1: Start with the Literal Image

Before learning the idiom, picture what the words literally mean.

Imagine you are sitting at a table and there are some crumbs on it. You don't care about them. You simply sweep your hand across the table and push them away in one quick, effortless motion. You didn't examine the crumbs. You didn't think twice about them. You just... got rid of them.

That physical action — quick, dismissive, effortless — is the heart of this idiom.
Step 2: The Idiomatic Meaning

"Brush aside" means to refuse to take something seriously, to dismiss it quickly, or to treat it as if it is unimportant or not worth your attention.

Just like brushing crumbs off a table without a second thought, when someone "brushes aside" something, they push it out of their mind quickly and move on — without truly engaging with it, addressing it, or giving it the respect it may deserve.

Think of it this way:

Someone raises a concern → You don't acknowledge it → You move on as if it wasn't said.

That is "brushing aside."
Step 3: What Can You "Brush Aside"?

This idiom is very flexible. You can brush aside many kinds of things:

Concerns or worries
Someone tells you something might go wrong. You say "don't worry about it" and move forward.

Criticism
Someone points out your mistakes. You dismiss what they said and continue doing what you were doing.

Objections or opposition
Someone disagrees with your plan. You ignore their disagreement and proceed anyway.

Suggestions or advice
Someone offers you an idea. You treat it as useless without really considering it.

A person's feelings or words
Someone tries to tell you something important to them. You don't take them seriously.

An obstacle (slightly different shade of meaning)
When used with a physical or competitive obstacle, "brush aside" means to overcome it very easily, as if it were nothing. For example, a powerful team might "brush aside" a weaker opponent — meaning they defeated them quickly and without much effort.
Step 4: The Key Feeling Behind the Idiom

The most important thing to understand about "brush aside" is the attitude it describes. It carries a sense of:

  • Dismissiveness — "This is not worth my time."
  • Superiority — "I know better. What you're saying doesn't matter."
  • Effortlessness — The person does it quickly, without struggle.

This is why the idiom often has a slightly negative tone. The person doing the "brushing aside" is usually seen as inconsiderate, overconfident, or unwilling to listen. When a writer or journalist says someone "brushed aside" a concern, it often implies that perhaps they shouldn't have brushed it aside — that the concern deserved more attention.

However, in the sports/competition sense (easily defeating an opponent), it is neutral or even positive — it simply means someone won easily.
Step 5: Real-Life Example Sentences

Read these carefully. Notice how the same core meaning appears in different situations.

In politics:
"The prime minister brushed aside questions about the scandal and changed the topic."
→ The prime minister dismissed the questions quickly and refused to engage with them.

In a personal relationship:
"Every time I tried to talk about my feelings, he just brushed them aside."
→ He didn't take her feelings seriously and moved on without addressing them.

At work:
"The manager brushed aside all concerns about the project deadline."
→ The manager ignored the concerns as if they weren't important.

In a competition or sport:
"The champion brushed aside her opponent in just 20 minutes."
→ She defeated her opponent easily and quickly, as if it were effortless.

About advice:
"She brushed aside her doctor's advice and continued her old habits."
→ She dismissed the doctor's advice without truly considering it.
Step 6: Grammar — How to Use It Correctly

"Brush aside" is a phrasal verb, and it is transitive, which means it always needs an object (something being brushed aside). Here is how to position that object:

Rule 1: A noun phrase can go after "aside" OR between "brush" and "aside."

✅ She brushed aside my concerns. (noun after)
✅ She brushed my concerns aside. (noun in the middle)

Both are perfectly correct. The meaning is identical.

Rule 2: A pronoun (him, her, it, them) MUST go in the middle — never after.

✅ She brushed them aside.
❌ She brushed aside them. ← This is wrong.

So if you replace the noun with a pronoun, always put it between "brush" and "aside."
Step 7: Common Variations

You will see "brush aside" used in different grammatical forms. Here are the most common ones:

  • brushed aside (past tense) — He brushed aside the criticism.
  • brushes aside (present, he/she/it) — She always brushes aside my ideas.
  • brushing aside (present participle) — Brushing aside all objections, he continued.
  • brush aside (base form) — Don't brush aside what I'm saying.
Step 8: Words That Mean the Same Thing (Synonyms)

If you want to say the same thing with different words, you can use:

  • dismiss — the most direct synonym
  • wave off — informal, same idea
  • shrug off — to treat something as unimportant
  • disregard — to pay no attention to
  • overlook — to deliberately ignore
  • pay no heed to — a more formal way of saying "ignore"
  • pooh-pooh — informal and slightly humorous; to treat something with contempt
Step 9: Opposite Meanings (Antonyms)

If you want to say the opposite of "brush aside," you could say:

  • take seriously
  • acknowledge
  • address
  • face up to
  • confront
  • engage with
  • give weight to
Step 10: Formal or Informal?

"Brush aside" works in both formal and informal contexts. You'll find it in:

  • Newspaper and magazine articles (very common)
  • Professional conversations
  • Everyday speech
  • Academic writing

It is not slang. It is a standard, widely-used English idiom that is appropriate in almost any setting.
Quick Summary (The Short Version)

"Brush aside" means to dismiss something quickly and treat it as unimportant — refusing to give it proper attention or consideration. The image behind it is the simple, effortless act of sweeping something away with your hand, as if it's nothing. When used in competition, it means to defeat someone easily.

Now you have everything you need — the origin, the meaning, the grammar, the examples, the tone, the synonyms, and the antonyms. You're fully equipped to understand this idiom whenever you encounter it and to use it confidently yourself.

Imagine you have dust or crumbs on your jacket. What do you do? You flick them away with your hand — quickly, casually, without a second thought. They're unimportant. Gone. Forgotten.

That one physical image is the heart of "brush off."

Now take that same action and apply it to a person, an idea, a warning, or a question instead of dust — and you have the figurative meaning that makes this phrase so widely used.

1. The Literal Meaning (physical)

In its most basic, physical sense, to brush off means to remove something from a surface by sweeping it away with your hand or a brush.

She brushed the sand off her feet before entering the house.
He brushed the crumbs off the table.

This is the original, concrete meaning. You'll use it occasionally, but it's not why this phrase is famous.

2. The Figurative Meaning (the main one)

This is what people almost always mean when they say "brush off." It means:

To dismiss someone or something quickly, casually, and without giving it the attention or respect it deserves.

Just like you flick away dust as if it's nothing — you do the same to a person or an idea. You treat them as unimportant, insignificant, or not worth your time.

It carries a feeling of coldness, indifference, or rudeness.
Breaking the Figurative Meaning Into Two Directions

"Brush off" works in two closely related ways:

Direction 1 — Brushing off a PERSON

This means you dismiss, reject, or ignore someone — often coldly or abruptly — when they try to talk to you, ask for your help, or get your attention.

When the student raised her hand to ask a question, the professor brushed her off and moved on.
(= He dismissed her; he didn't give her time or attention.)

She's been trying to reach him for a week, but he keeps brushing her off.
(= He keeps ignoring her or giving her short, dismissive responses.)

I tried to introduce myself, but he brushed me off.
(= He rejected my attempt to connect; he was cold and uninterested.)

The person being brushed off usually feels unwelcome, rejected, or belittled. It's not a pleasant experience.

Direction 2 — Brushing off a THING (a concern, a comment, a warning, criticism, etc.)

This means you treat an idea, a problem, or a concern as if it's not worth thinking about. You dismiss it as trivial, unimportant, or not serious — often when it actually is serious.

The doctor brushed off her concerns about the pain and told her to rest.
(= He treated her concerns as unimportant and didn't investigate properly.)

The manager brushed off all criticism of the project.
(= He refused to take the criticism seriously or consider it.)

He brushed off the warning signs and continued driving.
(= He ignored the warnings and moved on as if they didn't matter.)

She brushed off the bad review, saying the critic didn't understand her work.
(= She dismissed it without letting it bother her.)

Important nuance here: Sometimes brushing off a thing (not a person) can actually be positive — like when someone brushes off a small failure and keeps going. For example:

He brushed off the setback and got back to work.
(= He didn't let a small problem discourage him. He moved on.)

So when applied to things, brushing off can be either negative (dismissing something important) or positive (not being affected by something minor). Context tells you which one it is.

The phrase also works as a noun, usually written with a hyphen: the brush-off.

It refers to the act of being dismissed or rejected.

I called her three times and she didn't answer. I think she's giving me the brush-off.
(= She's rejecting/ignoring me.)

He went to speak to the director, but he got the brush-off.
(= He was dismissed quickly and coldly.)

After three unanswered emails, I took the hint — it was clearly a brush-off.

The noun form is used when you want to name the experience of being dismissed. "The brush-off" is that cold, quick rejection.
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

"Brush off" is a phrasal verb, which means it's a verb ("brush") combined with a particle ("off") to create a new meaning.

Here's how it works grammatically:

When the object is a noun, you can place it either in the middle or at the end:

She brushed off the question. ✅
She brushed the question off. ✅ (Both are correct.)

When the object is a pronoun (him, her, it, me, them), it must go in the middle — never at the end:

She brushed it off. ✅
She brushed him off. ✅
She brushed off it. ❌ (This is wrong.)
She brushed off him. ❌ (This is wrong.)
The Tone and Feeling Behind "Brush Off"

This phrase almost always carries a negative emotional charge — especially when it's about a person being brushed off. It suggests:

  • Disrespect — the person being brushed off is not valued.
  • Indifference — no effort is made to engage with them.
  • Coldness — the dismissal is quick and impersonal.
  • Superiority — the one doing the brushing often acts as if the other person is beneath their attention.

Think of it like being treated as an annoyance — like a fly someone swats away.

These words and phrases are close to "brush off" in meaning, though each has slight differences:

  • Dismiss — the most neutral and formal equivalent. ("He dismissed her concerns.")
  • Shrug off — to act unbothered by something, often with more ease or confidence. ("She shrugged off the criticism.")
  • Brush aside — almost identical to "brush off"; used interchangeably. ("He brushed aside all objections.")
  • Wave off — to dismiss something with a gesture of the hand; slightly more casual. ("She waved off the suggestion.")
  • Rebuff — a more formal word specifically for rejecting a person. ("His offer was rebuffed.")
  • Blow off — very informal; means to ignore or cancel on someone. ("He blew off the meeting.")
What Makes "Brush Off" Different From "Give the Cold Shoulder"?

Both phrases involve ignoring or dismissing someone, but there's a difference:

  • "Brush off" is usually a single, quick act of dismissal — in a moment, in a conversation.
  • "Give the cold shoulder" is a more sustained form of ignoring someone — a pattern of behavior over time, often done to show disapproval.

He brushed her off when she tried to speak to him. (one moment)
He gave her the cold shoulder for an entire week. (ongoing behavior)
Real-Life Situations Where You'd Hear This

• A politician ignoring a journalist's tough question.
  • A busy parent dismissing a child's worries without listening.
  • A doctor not taking a patient's symptoms seriously.
  • A coworker rejecting your ideas in a meeting without discussion.
  • Someone ignoring your texts or phone calls.
  • An athlete shaking off a poor performance and moving forward.

FormExample
Verb (person)Don't brush me off — I have something important to say.
Verb (thing)He brushed off all the warnings.
NounShe gave him the brush-off.

To put it in one sentence: "Brush off" means to dismiss someone or something quickly and carelessly, as if they don't matter — just like flicking dust off your sleeve.

A brushstroke is the mark or trace that a paintbrush leaves on a surface in a single, continuous movement. Think of it this way: every time a painter dips a brush in paint and sweeps it across a canvas, paper, or wall — that one sweep, and the visible mark it creates — is a brushstroke.

It is both the action (the sweeping movement of the brush) and the result (the mark that remains after that movement). In its noun form, it most commonly refers to the visible mark itself.

Imagine you dip a brush in blue paint and drag it across a white canvas from left to right. You have just made one brushstroke. Now look at what's left on the canvas — that streak of blue paint, with its particular shape, width, texture, and direction — that is the brushstroke.

A finished painting is essentially a collection of hundreds, thousands, or even millions of individual brushstrokes layered and arranged together.
What a Brushstroke Can Look Like

Brushstrokes are not all the same. They vary enormously, and those differences carry meaning. A single brushstroke can be:

  • Long or short — a long, sweeping stroke across the canvas vs. a tiny dab in one spot
  • Thick or thin — depending on how much paint is on the brush and how much pressure the painter applies
  • Smooth or rough — a gentle stroke leaves clean, soft edges; a heavy, quick stroke can leave jagged, textured edges
  • Straight or curved — a stroke can glide in a straight line, arc in a curve, or twist and swirl
  • Visible or invisible — some painters blend their strokes so carefully that you cannot see individual marks; others leave strokes boldly visible so you can see every single one

In art, brushstrokes are far more than just a technical necessity. They are one of the primary ways a painter expresses personality, emotion, and style.

Vincent van Gogh, for example, is famous for his wild, swirling, thick brushstrokes — if you look at his painting The Starry Night, you can clearly see each bold, energetic stroke of paint. Those strokes make the sky feel as if it is moving. Claude Monet, on the other hand, used short, feathery brushstrokes placed side by side to create the impression of shimmering light on water. In both cases, the brushstroke is not just a tool — it is the art.

Because of this, brushstrokes are often studied to understand an artist's technique, mood, and identity. Art experts can sometimes identify who painted an unsigned painting simply by examining its brushstrokes, the same way you might recognize someone's handwriting.

Outside of painting, the word brushstroke is used figuratively to mean a single detail, action, or element that contributes to a larger whole — especially when describing something created with skill or artistry.

For example:

  • "The director added the final brushstrokes to the film before its release." — Here, "brushstrokes" means the last finishing touches or refinements, as if the director were a painter completing a canvas.
  • "With a few bold brushstrokes, the author painted a vivid picture of life in ancient Rome." — Here, "brushstrokes" means skillfully chosen words or details that together create a strong impression, just as paint strokes create an image.
  • "The new policy was designed with broad brushstrokes, leaving the details for later." — Here, "broad brushstrokes" means a general, high-level outline — the big shapes and ideas, without the fine details filled in yet.

This figurative use is very common in English, especially when talking about writing, planning, design, filmmaking, or any creative or intellectual work.

This phrase deserves extra attention because it is used very frequently. Broad brushstrokes (or broad brush strokes) refers to a way of describing or dealing with something in general, sweeping terms — without going into specifics or nuance.

  • "She explained the plan in broad brushstrokes." — She gave a general overview, not a detailed breakdown.
  • "The report paints all immigrants with broad brushstrokes." — The report treats all immigrants as if they are the same, ignoring individual differences (this is often used critically, to suggest oversimplification or unfairness).

The logic is simple: a broad stroke of a brush covers a lot of ground quickly but lacks precision and fine detail. A narrow, careful stroke is more exact. So "broad brushstrokes" = big, general, imprecise.

• "You could see each individual brushstroke in the old oil painting."
  • "Her brushstrokes were confident and bold — she never hesitated."
  • "The artist's brushstrokes became more frantic toward the end of the painting."
  • "The architect sketched out the building's design in broad brushstrokes."
  • "Every brushstroke in the portrait was deliberate and precise."
The plural is simply brushstrokes — used when referring to more than one mark or, in the figurative sense, more than one detail or element.

If you had to remember one thing:

A brushstroke is the single mark a paintbrush makes in one movement, and by extension, any one small but deliberate detail or action that contributes to something larger. It can be literal (a mark of paint on canvas) or figurative (a detail that shapes a bigger picture). The word captures the idea of craft, intention, and individuality — because no two brushstrokes, like no two fingerprints, are ever exactly the same.
